column1: # Expected values for the X.509 certificates the fetched corpora carry, one
# per line, tab-separated.
# WHERE THESE NUMBERS COME FROM, AND WHY THAT MATTERS
# Milestone 2 of docs/design/signatures.md asks for "the subject/issuer/
# validity/SPKI values committed in its sidecar, transcribed once from the
# certificate's own DER and reviewed". Transcribing by hand from a hex dump is
# how the RFC 5280 appendix certificates were done and it does not scale to
# twenty-four; producing them with `tinker-pdf-pki` would be the parser
# agreeing with itself, which is the one thing a sidecar must not be.
# So they were produced ONCE by OpenSSL 3.5.5 (27 Jan 2026) on 28 August 2026,
# and committed. Ruling 13 permits exactly this and no more: a third-party
# program may supply data, and the committed output of a tool that was run
# once is a dated measurement rather than a check. Nothing re-runs OpenSSL;
# `cargo xtask oracles` would refuse a test that tried.
# The commands, for anyone regenerating them:
#   openssl x509 -inform DER -in <cert> -noout #     -subject -issuer -serial -startdate -enddate -nameopt RFC2253
#   openssl x509 -inform DER -in <cert> -noout -pubkey #     | openssl pkey -pubin -outform DER | sha256sum
# The certificates themselves are NOT here: they come from corpora that
# `corpus/corpora.lock` pins by hash and that nothing from ever enters git
# (corpus/README.md). `sha256` identifies each one, so a row that stops
# matching any certificate is a corpus that moved and says so.
# FIELDS
#   sha256       of the certificate's DER, which is the key
#   serial       the INTEGER's content octets, uppercase hex, read from the
#                DER by an independent scanner rather than taken from OpenSSL
#                THREE OF THESE DIFFER FROM WHAT OPENSSL PRINTS, and the
#                difference is a real one about real certificates. Their top
#                bit is set with no leading zero, so the serial *is* a negative
#                INTEGER in DER — RFC 5280 4.1.2.2 says it "MUST be a positive
#                integer" and those issuers emitted one that is not. OpenSSL
#                reads the number and prints `-0603E746C0C547A1789F`; this
#                crate does the same. The octets `F9FC18B93F3AB85E8761` are
#                what `issuerAndSerialNumber` matching actually compares, so
#                they are what is recorded here — the identity rather than
#                either side's rendering of the value.
#   not_before   validity start, seconds since the Unix epoch
#   not_after    validity end, the same
#   spki_sha256  of the DER of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo
#   self_issued  whether subject and issuer render identically
#   subject_cn   the subject's common name, or empty where it has none
#   issuer_cn    the issuer's
# Two fields are deliberately absent. The full distinguished names are not
# compared, because RFC 4514 leaves the escaping of several characters to the
# renderer and two correct implementations disagree about them — a difference
# that would make this file a test of string formatting rather than of
# parsing. The public key's own modulus is not compared either; the SPKI
# digest covers it and cannot be satisfied by a partly-right answer.
